subject: snow
title: What If You Ate Snow to Stay Hydrated?

scenes.text: What if you were lost in the cold and ate snow for water? It's a trap.
Fresh snow is mostly air. It often takes about ten cups of snow to make one cup of water.
Then your body has to melt it. Every liter takes about 80 calories just to turn into water, plus more to warm it up.
That heat comes from your core, right when you're already cold, and the ice can injure your lips and mouth.
City snow is worse. A 2017 McGill study found it soaks up exhaust particles and toxic hydrocarbons.
So military survival manuals say it plainly: do not eat snow. Melt it first. The water is free. The heat isn't.

description:
What if you ate snow to stay hydrated? Fresh snow is mostly air, with a common snow-to-water ratio around 10 or 12 to 1, and melting ice takes 334 joules per gram, about 80 calories per litre, before warming it to body temperature.
The US military survival manual says do not eat ice or snow because it lowers body temperature and can injure the mouth; melt it first. A McGill study found urban snow absorbs pollutants from car exhaust.
